**Fig. 1** Study design. Ten detectors saw only the first 3–6 visual-field tests of each eye. They were evaluated against a future-confirmed reference in the held-out UWHVF test set (E1), on true no-change series from patients tested weekly for 12 weeks (E2, Artes retest data), with a shuffle audit of UWHVF test-set eyes (E3) and in an external clinic with clinician progression labels (E4, GRAPE). UWHVF, University of Washington Humphrey Visual Field data set; ML, machine learning.

**Fig. 2** Sensitivity for future-confirmed progression against the false-alarm rate on true no-change series, for 3, 4, 5 and 6 tests. Each point is one detector (D1–D10, see Methods); bars are patient-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. The shaded area marks false-alarm rates at or below the nominal 5% (dashed line). Detectors to the right of the line flag more progressors only by raising more false alarms. Note the different x-axis scales.

**Fig. 3** Shuffle audit against the true false-alarm rate. Each point is one detector at one number of tests (3–6). The x-axis shows the share of UWHVF test-set eyes flagged after their first k tests were randomly re-ordered (shuffle audit); the y-axis shows the share of true no-change series flagged (Artes retest data). The dashed line marks perfect agreement. Points below the line: the audit over-estimates false alarms; points above: it under-estimates them.

**Fig. 4** External clinic (GRAPE, Hangzhou, China): sensitivity against 1 − specificity for the clinicians' mean-deviation progression label, using the first 3 (left) or 4 (right) tests. Bars are patient-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. D5 and D7 were re-calibrated on GRAPE by cross-fitting; D8 was transferred unchanged from UWHVF; D6, D9 and D10 were not applicable. Note the different x-axis scales.
